Rack of ribs. St. Louis, not baby back. SL has more meat on it.

Brussel Sprouts

Sweet potatoes.

All you need is a large baking pan. Coat the ribs with olive oil, kosher salt and cracked pepper. Same for brussel sprouts and sweet potato slices.

Put the ribs on the pan.

Cut the brussel sprouts in half. Oil, salt, and pepper them.

Slice the sweet potato around 1/4"-1/2" slices. Oil, salt, and pepper.

Put everything on a baking sheet. Just spread it out. Or you can you two baking sheets. One for veggies, and one for ribs.

Pop the sheets in a 350-degree oven for 50 minutes. The brussel sprouts will be crispy.

Take it out and serve immediately. To cut the ribs, turn them over and just cut between the bones.

The sprouts and sweet potatoes are an amazing combo together.

If you have some BBQ sauce or something else you like, like Teriyaki sauce, slather it on at the table.

I promise. It's super easy. All cooks at once, and for the same amount of time. And only have to use on two baking sheets.

Hardly any clean up.

This will blow your friends and family away.

FWIW, ALWAYS use Kosher salt when cooking. Never table salt.

I make fondu. I learned how when I was 17. It's basically 4 ingredients heated on a stove served with veggies and bread.

Cheese: emmental (you could replace this with swiss but I like this better) and gruyere (you can find this at a variety of places, my Safeway and Trader Joes both have it) - I usually use like 1.5 handfuls of grated cheese(this is seriously the hardest part, grating some cheese), it's fucking hard to measure cheese.

Other: 1/2 cup of dry white wine (don't bother spending more than 5 dollars unless you want to drink the rest or serve it with the meal), some garlic (to taste, 1 clove seems okay), and the most important ingredient that will mix the cheese and the oils and wine - cornstarch - put a bit of cornstarch in a bit of wine until it gets that liquid solid consistancy (you only need a table spoon so don't make too much).

Dump everything but the cornstarch concoction in a sauce pan, you know the one with high sides, and stir with a wooden spoon until it looks like the cheese has melted, if you want to be fancy stir in a figure 8 motion (not sure what this does but angry swiss chef told me this was the only correct way). Don't worry if it looks oily and not looking right. That is where the cornstarch magic happens. Take about a tablespoon of that mixture you made earlier and drizzle it into the cheese, keep stirring, you should now see the cheese and oil (from the cheese) and wine start coming together to make that creamy cheese like consistency, keep stirring it might take a few more stirs for everything to mix.

Serving: If you don't have a fancy fondue set up that's totally fine you can just put the pan on a trivet (don't wanna burn the table) and use regular forks. Put some crunchy bread chunks on a plate and some fresh broccoli or whatever veggies you like, heck pickles work too, now EAT. If it starts to solidify just throw it on the stove for a minute.

If you want to get a little bit fancier you can buy a sterno heater (thrift stores usually have them) and use that to keep the fondue warm while eating it.

Next level shit: Wine fondue (which you can use that leftover white wine from cheese fondue) which is white wine and little oil and water, some chicken seasoning, garlic, chives and whatever to make a yummy broth and you serve this with raw veggies and chicken and people get to cook their food at the table (this does require a sterno heater to keep the liquid at a temperature that will cook chicken). Traditionally served with 3 sauces - A mild creamy sauce like yogurt, spices, a mustard sauce that is a bit spicy, and a red sauce that might have cumin in it or something else you like.

That's a great question, and not vague at all. I think part of the trick to understanding good food is to have experience eating good food. Go out to eat at places that make good food. Doesn't even have to be expensive.

Also, use whole foods, and get fresh stuff. Shop mostly around the perimeter of the grocery store, and stay away from too much canned and processed stuff.

Basically: buy good stuff, and then just don't fuck it up. A lot of good cooking is much simpler than some people think. It's all about not overdoing it. Let the foods you buy work for you.

What are your suggestions for when you don't have a lot of time to spend cooking? (IE Only 20 minutes to put dinner on the table, what do you do?)

Well, 20 minutes is sort of the magic time for a lot of foods, including starches like pasta, potatoes, rice, etc.. But, you do need to get the pot boiling first.

Chicken and pork are out, since they take at least 40 minutes. Although pork tenderloin can be sliced and seared very quickly.

Beef is a good quick food. Ground beef can be cooked on a pan in about 10 minutes. Steaks take about 15 total.

If I want to do something quick, I like to do something where I just use one pan—like a cast iron skillet.

Seafood can be pretty quick. Some fishes like haddock, swai, and even frozen uncooked shrimp can all be made in under 10 minutes.

Sauted mushrooms and squash is really quick. Cook spinach in butter in about 10 minutes.

Omletes are quick.

Hmm, thinking super quick: Then don't do starches like potatoes, rice, pasta. Although, thinly sliced potatoes can fry up in a bit of oil in 10 minutes. Don't do chicken or pork, either.

Think throwing it all together on a pan. Beef, mushrooms, squash, onions, tomato, egg. Have nice bread and unsalted butter as the starch. And make a nice quick salad with whatever's around.
